Just before seven Abigail's phone finally does something — not their father calling back, but the building's rent office, an automated blue-tape reminder blast that goes to every unit in 114 Elm: BALANCE DUE 3B $1,140 BY THE 15TH. She goes to the coffee table where Max's briefs and lanyard and receipt are still laid out squared like evidence, and she does not clear them — she moves them, all of it, three inches to the left to make room, and sets her phone down in the cleared space with the rent text open on the screen, face up, angled at his bedroom door. Emily's hand meets his, brief and light, fingers loose before she draws back for the hug. Emily leans back, still holding the piece of bread, and finally eats it. She wipes her fingers on the napkin one at a time.

"Me. Okay." She reaches for the glass of water instead of the wine list, turns it a quarter turn on the tablecloth. "I do billing for a dental practice on Fourth, three dentists, one of them's actually the guy's son who bought the whole thing off the first guy, so technically I've had two bosses in the same chair for six years." She says it fast, like she's said it before. "Before that I did billing for a HVAC outfit, and before that I was still living at my grandmother's, over in Bayonne, and my uncle — I mentioned him — he ran supers for like twenty buildings over there, and he used to bring me on rounds sometimes when I was a kid, so I know more about boiler pressure than a person doing dental billing should know."

She breaks another piece of bread, doesn't eat it yet.

She looks him over once, not lingering, more like checking a delivery against a list.

"Four, daily, okay, that's — that's a real number, that's not the bullshit number." She says it almost to herself, checking it against something.

She picks a piece of bread off the pile that's left, tears it instead of eating it, sets the torn half down without touching it to her mouth.
